title: NASA's Astronaut Hub Prepares for Commercial Space Stations
summary:
As the International Space Station (ISS) approaches its retirement around 2030, NASA is already preparing for the next era of human spaceflight. A recent tour of Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston revealed how the agency is partnering with private industry to keep astronauts flying.

NASA's Commercial LEO Destinations (CLD) program aims to have private space stations ready by the time the ISS retires. In 2021, NASA awarded about $415 million in early-stage contracts to three teams led by Nanoracks, Blue Origin, and Northrop Grumman. Companies like Vast Space are also developing their own self-funded modules.

The tour included a visit to the iconic ISS Mission Control, where flight controllers monitor the Expedition 75 crew. Flight director Diane Dailey explained how they use a live camera view to assess the astronauts' workload before making calls. "We usually have that live camera view just up for awareness. It just helps us understand," she said.

Mission Control is a prime example of the "division of labor" that will be crucial for future space stations. "You're going to see different consoles that specialize in different aspects of spacecraft operations," Dailey noted. "You'd need propulsion. You'd need communications. You'd need computers. All of those things."

The Space Vehicle Mockup Facility, known as Building 9, is another key part of astronaut training. It's constantly in flux, with modules shifting in and out for different missions. The facility supports not only NASA missions but also private industry, providing space and hardware to simulate problems in space.

NASA officials emphasized that they are prepared to offer expertise and help to any company hosting astronauts. The agency is also learning "lessons learned" from the ISS to apply to future commercial stations.

While the ISS has had a leak on the Russian side, NASA says the situation is under control after Roscosmos agreed to seal off that area. Major station systems are otherwise in good health.

As the space industry evolves, Johnson Space Center remains at the heart of human spaceflight, bridging government and private efforts to explore the cosmos.
why_it_matters: The transition from a government-owned station to privately run stations may decide how many countries, researchers, and astronauts can access low Earth orbit in the future. If private stations are late or too expensive, access to space could narrow rather than expand.

background_read: The International Space Station, a multinational research outpost in low Earth orbit, has been continuously occupied by rotating crews since 2000; its hardware is aging as its planned retirement approaches 2030.
Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, is NASA's main center for human spaceflight, astronaut training, and Mission Control.
NASA's Commercial LEO Destinations program is meant to encourage private companies to build replacements for the ISS rather than NASA owning and operating the next station itself.
In 2021, NASA gave early-stage contracts to three teams led by Nanoracks, Blue Origin, and Northrop Grumman, all private aerospace companies with different station concepts.
Vast Space, another private firm, is also developing its own self-funded modules outside the main contract.
Roscosmos, Russia's state space corporation, operates Russia's part of the ISS and has worked with NASA on recent issues such as a sealed leak on its side.
This follows a broader shift in which NASA increasingly pays private companies for transportation and experiments instead of owning all hardware.

perspectives.description: Private space stations could lower costs and expand opportunities for research, manufacturing, and tourism in orbit. Competition among companies such as Blue Origin, Nanoracks, and Northrop Grumman may speed innovation.

Relying on commercial providers may prioritize profit over safety, affordability, or broad access. There is no guarantee that private stations will be ready by 2030, which could create a gap in low Earth orbit operations.

NASA's shift follows a procurement model already used for cargo and crew transportation, in which the agency buys services rather than owning hardware. This changes who controls space infrastructure and how oversight is divided between government and industry.

The years before 2030 will test whether multiple commercial stations can be built, staffed, and sustained. How NASA manages the transition will shape the next generation of human spaceflight and international partnerships.
